description: We’re a team of three tackling Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions. On a deep-space mission, a message to Earth can take several minutes to arrive, so when a crewmate collapses, the crew has to act on its own. Our app helps astronauts check their own health every day on a live, color-coded body map.
summary:
Health Co-Pilot is an on-board health assistant that helps astronauts spot problems early and act fast when help is far away.

A body map shows heart, lungs, brain and mood, metabolism, immune system, bones and radiation, colour-coded Nominal, Watch, Warning or Act now. Every reading is compared to the astronaut’s own baseline, with a forecast of when a slow drift becomes critical. It covers all the indicators in the challenge (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood) plus oxygen, breathing, cabin CO₂ and radiation. For each problem it explains what to do, who to tell, and why it happens in space, and drafts a message to the flight surgeon.

In emergencies, an alarm opens step-by-step collapse and chest-pain protocols with cited sources, including guided CPR. An on-device camera detects an unresponsive crewmate who drifts limp in microgravity, and a PPG pulse sensor (median error 0.86 bpm on 53 hospital recordings) tracks heart rate.

It runs fully offline on the ISS, a Moon base, Mars transit or a surface rover, using real NASA and CSA data. Because communication delays grow with distance, crews need to be their own first responders.
details:
Live demo: https://nasa-space-app-2026-red.vercel.app/
Code: https://github.com/jionchoi/nasa-space-app-2026

What it does

Health Co-Pilot is an on-board health monitoring and guidance app for astronauts. It answers three questions all day: How am I doing? What should I do? What if something goes wrong?

  • Body map dashboard: a human figure with labelled areas (brain and mood, heart, lungs and air, immune system, metabolism, bones and muscles, radiation). Each area glows by status: Nominal, Watch, Warning or Act now. A badge shows how many areas need attention.
  • Personal baselines and forecasts: each reading is compared to the astronaut’s own usual (the first 14 days), not a population average. Trends are projected forward, for example “At this pace: Act now in about 12 days.”
  • Guidance: for every area, What to do (a checklist), Who to tell (self → crew → flight surgeon → return to base on a rover → emergency), and a Learn pop-up explaining how it’s measured, why it changes in space, and how to stay healthy.
  • Daily routine: a daily health check (pulse, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, mood and symptoms, reaction test), meal, water and exercise logging, reminders and a streak.
  • Emergencies: an Act now alarm, then step-by-step collapse and chest-pain protocols with yes/no branches, cited guidelines, and guided CPR (metronome, rescuer switching, microgravity positioning). Everything is logged automatically, and a message to the flight surgeon is drafted from the data.
  • Unresponsive detection: in orbit an unconscious astronaut doesn’t fall; they drift limp. An on-device camera checks whether the limbs are still moving relative to the body. If not, it asks “Are you OK?” and alerts the crew. Fall detection switches on only where there’s gravity.
  • PPG pulse sensing: an optical pulse pipeline turns the PPG waveform into pulse rate and variability, with quality checks that grey out bad readings instead of guessing.
  • Locations: ISS, Moon base, Mars transit, and a surface rover on the Moon or Mars. Each has its own radiation source and communication delay.

How it works

A FastAPI backend streams vitals over WebSockets, applies the health rules (the single source of status), stores logs in SQLite, and runs the PPG pipeline. A React frontend shows the dashboard, timeline, charts and emergency mode. Everything runs offline on board. A public demo build runs entirely in the browser with simulated data.

NASA and space-agency data

  • Radiation: NASA RadLab DOSTEL1 (ISS) and Curiosity MSL-RAD (Mars), both real data. Moon and Mars-transit values are clearly labelled estimates.
  • Cabin CO₂, temperature and humidity: the NASA Environmental Data App.
  • Solar storms: NASA DONKI (replay of the May 2024 event, which triggers a shelter alert).
  • Crew comparison: the Inspiration4 metabolic panel from NASA OSDR (OSD-575).
  • Reaction-time norms: the CSA PRET study (145 participants).
  • PPG validation: PhysioNet BIDMC (53 records) and the PhysioNet Challenge 2015 data.

Medical basis

Our medical lead built the thresholds and protocols from NASA-STD-3001 (Volumes 1 and 2), NASA Human Research Program evidence, AHA, ADA, NCRP, FDA guidance and spaceflight studies: 17 references in total. Every rule is labelled “proposed, not clinically validated”. Some signals (heart rate variability, the reaction test, biomarkers) never trigger an emergency alone, and the app never prescribes drugs or doses.

Benefits and impact

  • Catches slow problems (fluid shift, sleep loss, deconditioning) days early.
  • Gives clear, plain-language actions when the flight surgeon is minutes away.
  • Supports crew autonomy for Moon and Mars missions, and could support remote and austere settings on Earth.

Creativity

  • Detecting limpness instead of falls, because of microgravity.
  • A forecast of when a trend turns critical.
  • Delay-aware messages to the surgeon.
  • A rover mode with “return to base”.
  • Learning built into every alert.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts.
  • Camera: MediaPipe pose tracking in the browser.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, WebSockets, SQLite.
  • PPG: a Python signal-processing package using NumPy.
  • Design and slides: Claude Design and Canva. Hosting: Vercel. Code: GitHub.
  • Hardware: designed for a wearable PPG sensor plus a laptop or tablet camera. We validated on recorded signals.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: a person confirms each emergency step, and real sensor data never raises alarms by itself.
  • Honesty: real data and estimates are labelled, and limits are stated.
  • Offline operation: no internet is needed on board.
  • Privacy: camera video never leaves the device.
  • Accessibility: colours always come with text labels, plus keyboard shortcuts.
  • Microgravity physics.

Limitations

  • There’s no public in-flight astronaut PPG data, so we validated on Earth recordings.
  • No lost-pulse detection from the real sensor yet.
  • This is a prototype, not a medical device.

Team

  • Jion: app, camera detection, backend.
  • Jian: PPG signal processing.
  • Yenna: medical science, thresholds and protocols.

Disclaimer: We used Claude and Claude Code to help write code, documentation and design. The app itself makes no AI decisions; an optional “Polish wording” button for the surgeon message only works with an API key.
